papers.title: Multipliers and integration operators on Hardy--Bloch type tent spaces
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28895v1

summary.one_liner: The paper characterizes when integration operators J_g and I_g and pointwise multipliers M_g are bounded between Hardy–Bloch type tent spaces BT^p, with complete results for I_g and for J_g and M_g when p<q, and separate conditions when p≥q.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of function spaces made of holomorphic (complex-differentiable) functions on a disc, defined by controlling a maximal average of their derivative near the boundary. It asks when certain simple operations, such as integrating a function or multiplying it by a fixed function g, keep a function inside these spaces in a controlled way. The authors give a full answer for one operator across all exponents, and for the other two operators in one range of exponents, with separate but not fully matching conditions in the other range.
summary.why: Operators of this kind are a standard way to compare function spaces in complex analysis, so the results clarify how these spaces relate to each other. The text does not claim applications beyond this area, so any wider significance is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Holomorphic function: a complex-valued function that is complex-differentiable on an open region, here the unit disc.
- Bloch-type space: functions whose derivative is controlled (bounded in a weighted sense) near the boundary.
- Hardy space: a space of functions whose boundary behaviour is measured by an integral power p.
- Tent space: a space built from functions on the disc through a maximal function taken over cones ("tents") reaching the boundary.
- Non-tangential maximal function: the largest value a function takes over approach regions that meet the boundary at an angle, used to measure boundary behaviour.
- Integration operator J_g, I_g and multiplier M_g: operations that respectively integrate f against g, integrate f times g, or multiply f pointwise by g.
- Boundedness: the operator maps the space into the target space with output size controlled by input size.
- Fractional maximal function: a averaging tool that measures local size with a power-law weight; used as an estimate in the proofs.
- Exponents p, q: parameters indexing the spaces; p<q and p≥q are the two regimes treated differently.

papers.abstract: We investigate the boundedness of integration operators $J_g$ and $I_g$ and pointwise multipliers $M_g$ on Hardy--Bloch type tent spaces $\mathcal{BT}^p$. The main difficulty is that these spaces are defined through a non-tangential maximal function of the radial derivative, which places the problem at the interface of holomorphic function theory and harmonic analysis. We completely characterize the boundedness of $I_g:\mathcal{BT}^p\to\mathcal{BT}^q$ for all $0<p,q<\infty$, and obtain a complete characterization for $J_g$ and $M_g$ when $p<q$. For $p\geq q$, we establish separate necessary and sufficient conditions. The proofs in the case $p\leq q$ are mainly based on some fractional maximal function estimates, whereas those in the case $p>q$ are mainly based on a synthesis lemma. We also give examples showing that several converse implications in the range $p\geq q$ fail.

papers.title: Perturbed Nevo--Thangavelu maximal functions on two-step nilpotent groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28400v1

summary.one_liner: The paper studies L^p boundedness of maximal averages over parabolically dilated, curved convex hypersurfaces lying in a tilted subspace of a two-step nilpotent Lie group, in the low-rank regime, with a sharp range of p for m=1 and a Łojasiewicz-exponent criterion for m≥2.
summary.plain: The paper concerns a mathematical averaging tool: it looks at how averages of a function over curved surfaces, taken at many scales, can be controlled in size. The setting is a special kind of curved geometric space (a two-step nilpotent group, identified with ordinary coordinate space). The authors determine exactly which range of exponents p makes this averaging tool well behaved when the extra dimension m equals 1, and for m at least 2 they give a condition, stated through a Łojasiewicz exponent, for when a known necessary range is also enough.
summary.why: Maximal function bounds are a standard way to test how well averages behave, and sharp results of this kind shape the broader theory of averages on curved spaces. The text does not say more about applications, so the wider connections are uncertain from this excerpt alone.
summary.background:
- Maximal function: the supremum over many scales of averages of a function over a set; boundedness on L^p means the result stays controlled in an L^p size measure for inputs in that space.
- L^p spaces: a family of size measures indexed by p; the question is which p work.
- Nilpotent Lie group: a curved, non-commutative generalization of Euclidean space with layered (step-two) structure; exponential coordinates give it a concrete coordinate form.
- Parabolic dilates: scalings that stretch different coordinate directions by different amounts.
- Gaussian curvature: the product of principal curvatures of a surface; nonvanishing means the surface is curved everywhere in every direction.
- Tilted subspace: a flat slice of the space that is not aligned with the standard coordinate axes.
- Łojasiewicz exponent: a number measuring how flat or degenerate a real-analytic function is near its zeros, used here as a geometric quantity controlling the answer.

papers.abstract: Consider a step-two nilpotent Lie group $G$ identified with $\mathbb R^d\times \mathbb R^m$ in exponential coordinates. We study maximal operators associated with parabolic dilates of smooth convex hypersurfaces with nonvanishing Gaussian curvature in a tilted $d$-dimensional subspace of $G$. We focus on the low-rank regime, where the rank is determined by the group law and the tilt. When $m=1$, we determine the optimal range of $p$ for which the maximal operator is bounded on $L^p(G)$. For $m\ge2$, we characterize, in terms of a {\L}ojasiewicz exponent, when the known necessary condition on $p$ is also sufficient.

papers.title: On the Bourgain-Rudnick eigenfunction restriction conjecture in four dimensions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29806v1

summary.background:
- Flat torus: a space with no curvature that wraps around like a video game screen, in which opposite edges are glued together.
- Eigenfunction: a wave-like pattern that keeps its shape under the Laplace operator, roughly a standing wave with fixed frequency.
- L^2 norm: a way of measuring the overall size of a function; bounds on it limit how strongly waves can focus.
- Paraboloid: a curved bowl-shaped surface; here, a compact piece of it.
- Lattice point statistics: how integer grid points are distributed on a sphere, which relates to eigenfunction sizes.
- Fourier restriction: the study of how Fourier transforms behave when restricted to curved surfaces.
- Fractal restriction theorem: a result (by Du and Zhang) about how restriction estimates hold for sets with fractal-like spread.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a uniform L^2 upper bound for eigenfunctions of the four-dimensional flat torus restricted to the compact paraboloid, using Fourier restriction estimates and the Du–Zhang fractal restriction theorem applied on two-dimensional slices.
summary.plain: The paper studies the standing-wave patterns (eigenfunctions) that live on a four-dimensional flat, repeating space, and how much they can concentrate when measured on a curved surface inside that space. The authors prove an upper limit on that concentration, which is a version of a conjecture by Bourgain and Rudnick. Their method reinterprets counts of lattice points on spheres as a measure of how spread out certain points are, and then uses a known theorem about that spread.
summary.why: Bounds of this type control how large wave-like functions can get on a surface, a question that links number theory (lattice point counts) with analysis of waves. The text does not discuss applications beyond this setting, and it only mentions that further extensions are possible without specifying them.

papers.abstract: We prove a uniform upper $L^2$ bound for eigenfunctions of the four-dimensional flat torus on the compact paraboloid $\mathbb{P}^3$. The main novelty is the use of Fourier restriction estimates. We interpret spherical lattice point statistics as non-concentration inequalities of the strength needed to apply the Du--Zhang fractal restriction theorem. We apply their result on two-dimensional slices of $\mathbb{P}^3$. Further possible extensions are also discussed.

papers.title: The $T1$ theorem under Dini regularity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30870v1

summary.background:
- Harmonic analysis: the study of how functions decompose into waves or frequencies and how operators act on them.
- Singular integral operator: an averaging operator whose kernel blows up near the diagonal, so it needs careful treatment.
- Calderón-Zygmund operator: a major class of singular integral operators with kernel size and smoothness estimates.
- T1 theorem: a criterion saying such an operator is bounded if it is bounded on a test function like the constant 1 (plus related conditions).
- Dini regularity: a slightly weaker-than-Hölder smoothness condition on a function, measured by an integral condition on its modulus of continuity.
- Operator boundedness: the operator does not blow up the size of inputs beyond a fixed constant factor.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves the T1 theorem for Calderón-Zygmund operators assuming only the classical Dini regularity condition on the kernel, which the authors describe as resolving a long-standing open problem in singular integral theory.
summary.plain: The paper is about a standard test in harmonic analysis: a rule for deciding when an operator that smooths and rearranges functions stays well-behaved (bounded) when measured in standard size norms. The authors show this test works under the Dini condition, a classical smoothness requirement on the operator's kernel. The text states that this answers a question that had been open for a long time.
summary.why: The T1 theorem is a central tool for checking boundedness of singular integrals, which underlie much of modern analysis and partial differential equations. The provided text gives only the abstract, so its precise scope and how it compares with earlier results cannot be judged from it.

papers.abstract: We prove the $T1$ theorem for Calder\'on-Zygmund operators under the classical Dini regularity condition on the kernel, solving a longstanding open problem in singular integral theory.

papers.title: Freedom is all you need
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27943v1

summary.background:
- Functional calculus: a way of plugging a matrix or operator into a function (like a polynomial or power series) and getting a matrix or operator back.
- Matrices do not generally commute (AB may differ from BA), so "noncommutative" versions of these ideas are harder than the usual scalar case.
- Similarity (change of coordinates): rewriting a matrix in a different basis; a domain is "similarity invariant" if the property is preserved under such rewriting.
- Direct sum: stacking matrices block-diagonally.
- Category: an abstract framework of objects and maps between them, used here as the setting for the free calculus.
- Analyticity: a function that is locally given by a convergent power series; "monodromy" refers to how analytic continuation around loops can change a function.
- Overfitting: a machine learning model fitting training data very closely, including noise.
summary.one_liner: The paper begins a representation theory that relates a generic free functional calculus (for matrices and operators, over categories) to the classical noncommutative functional calculus of Taylor and Voiculescu, and notes consequences for domains that are closed under direct sums and similarity changes of coordinates.
summary.plain: The paper is about a way of applying functions to grids of numbers (matrices) and to more abstract operators, where the inputs can be non-commuting. It starts a general framework that links a newer "free" version of this calculus to the older classical version. The abstract only states that this framework is initiated and gives some properties of the resulting function classes; it does not give the detailed results.
summary.why: The abstract connects the framework to complex analysis and to large parallel networks, and it suggests a possible but explicitly "hypothetical" explanation for why overfitting can sometimes be harmless in such networks. That link is speculative as stated, and the text alone does not show how far it goes.

papers.abstract: The functional calculus allows for the rigorous analysis of functions of matrices or even operators. The free functional calculus gives the natural class of functions over any category. We initiate the representation theory for taking a generic free functional calculus to the classical nc functional calculus going back to Taylor, Voiculescu and many others, with an eye towards learning of categories. The functional calculus on direct sum closed and locally similarity (i.e. change of coordinates) invariant domains inherits the niceties of complex analysis and large-scale parallel networks, such as automatic analyticity, free universal monodromy, which gives a hypothetical explanation for beneficial overfitting.

papers.title: The Ritt problem is decidable
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27008v1

summary.background:
- Polynomials: sums of powers of a variable, such as x^2 + 3x.
- Functional decomposition: writing a function as a composition of simpler functions, e.g. f(g(x)).
- Ritt's theory: classical results by Joseph Ritt (1920s–1930s) on when and how such decompositions can be rearranged.
- Decidability: whether a yes/no question can be answered by a fixed, always-terminating algorithm.
- Harmonic analysis is the listed field, but the abstract itself concerns algebraic decomposition problems; the link is not explained in the text.
summary.one_liner: The paper claims a positive answer to the Ritt problem, which asks whether a certain algorithmic decision question about functional decompositions of polynomials and related functions is solvable.
summary.plain: This paper settles a long-standing question about how complicated formulas can be broken into simpler pieces. The Ritt problem asks whether there is a reliable procedure that can decide if two such breakdowns of a formula are equivalent. The text says the authors give a positive answer, meaning such a procedure exists, but the short summary does not spell out the method.
summary.why: The text is only a one-sentence abstract, so its importance cannot be judged from it alone. Results of this kind matter to researchers in algebra, dynamics and computer algebra, since they settle whether a class of questions can be answered by computation at all.

papers.abstract: We give an affirmative solution to the Ritt problem.

papers.title: Oscillatory integral operators of arbitrary signature: beyond the universal estimates
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26265v1

summary.background:
- Oscillatory integral operator: an integral whose kernel is a fast-oscillating exponential e^{i·phase}, used to measure how smoothing or spreading a function occurs.
- L^p bounds: statements that the operator keeps a function's size measured in the L^p norm within a constant factor, for a given exponent p.
- Signature of a phase: an integer-valued summary of the curvature of the phase function (how many directions curve positively versus negatively).
- Hörmander class: a standard family of phase functions with controlled smoothness and nondegeneracy assumptions.
- Fourier restriction conjecture: a central open problem asking how the Fourier transform of a function restricted to a curved surface behaves; Wang–Wu's recent work is a major advance on it.
- Universal range: the set of exponents p for which the estimate holds regardless of the particular phase, given its signature.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves L^p-to-L^p and sharp L^p-to-L^q bounds for Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on R^n, with constants that depend on the signature of the phase, under a non-compression hypothesis, in odd dimensions, using techniques from Wang–Wu's work on the Fourier restriction conjecture.
summary.plain: This paper studies a family of averaging operators that weight a function by a rapidly wiggling phase, a standard object in harmonic analysis. The authors ask how well these operators behave when the wiggling is described by a "signature," a count of how the phase curves in different directions. They show that, under a mild condition on the phase, some estimates can be pushed beyond the best previously known general range, but only in odd dimensions.
summary.why: Sharp bounds for oscillatory integrals feed into questions about Fourier restriction and related wave and dispersive equations, so improvements in this area matter to specialists. The text does not show wider applications, so beyond the specialist setting its reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We consider Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$. In particular, we are interested in proving bounds with dependence on the signature of the phase. The sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^p$ estimates was obtained for any given signature by the second author and Iliopoulou. Under the mild non-compression hypotheses on the phase introduced in Chen et al., we prove $L^p\to L^p$ estimates that go beyond this universal range in odd dimensions. We also obtain the sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^q$ estimates for odd $n$. The techniques are based on the breakthrough work of Wang--Wu on the Fourier restriction conjecture.

papers.title: Collineations of the diamond lattice in a Hilbert space
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25622v1

summary.background:
- Hilbert space: a complete space of vectors with inner products, generalizing ordinary geometry to infinite dimensions.
- Closed subspace: a linear slice of the space that is closed under limits.
- Orthogonal projection: the operator that drops a vector perpendicularly onto a subspace.
- Algebraic complement: a subspace that together with another subspace spans the whole space with no overlap, without requiring perpendicularity.
- Compact operator: a map that is "nearly finite-dimensional" in the sense that it turns bounded sets into nearly compact sets.
- Involution: an operator that equals its own inverse when applied twice.
- Lattice of subspaces and collineations: the diamond lattice is the four-element structure {0, M, N, whole space}; collineations are its structure-preserving maps.
summary.one_liner: Characterizes when two non-trivial closed subspaces M and N of a separable Hilbert space, with trivial intersection and dense sum, can be swapped by an invertible operator (which can be taken to be an involution), in terms of a common algebraic complement and compactness conditions on projections.
summary.plain: This paper is about pairs of "flat slices" (subspaces) inside an infinite-dimensional space of functions or vectors, and whether a single reversible transformation can swap them. The author gives a precise test for when such a swap exists. The test asks whether the two slices share a common way of being completed to the whole space, or equivalently checks certain compactness conditions on how the slices are projected.
summary.why: The result settles exactly when a symmetric swap of two subspaces is possible, and it shows the group of symmetries of this small lattice of subspaces is always complemented. It is a structural statement in operator theory; the text does not indicate applications beyond this area.

papers.abstract: Let $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ be non-trivial closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}=\{0\}$ and $\mathscr{M}+\mathscr{N}$ is dense in $\mathscr{H}$. We characterize when there exists an invertible operator on $\mathscr{H}$ which maps $\mathscr{M}$ onto $\mathscr{N}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ onto $\mathscr{M}$. We prove that such an operator exists if and only if $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ have a common algebraic complement. This happens if and only if either neither of the operators $(I-P)Q$ and $(I-Q)P$ is compact, or $P-Q$ is compact and $\dim(\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}^\perp)=\dim(\mathscr{M}^\perp\cap\mathscr{N})$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the orthogonal projections onto $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$. Moreover, the operator can be chosen to be an involution. Consequently, the group of collineations of the diamond lattice $\{\{0\},\mathscr{M},\mathscr{N},\mathscr{H}\}$ which fix $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ is always complemented in the group of all its collineations.

papers.title: Variational Estimates for the Hardy--Littlewood Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24180v1

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of points (vertices) joined by edges; "finite connected" means finitely many points, all reachable from each other.
- Maximal operator: for each point, take the largest average of the function over neighbourhoods centred there; this gives a new function.
- Edge variation: the total size of changes in a function's values across edges of the graph.
- Variational constant: a number bounding how much the maximal function's edge variation can exceed the original's.
- Star graph: one central point joined to several outer points.
- Exponent: a parameter p in the setting of function-size measures; results are stated for p greater than one.
- Extremizer: a function that makes the inequality as tight as possible.
summary.one_liner: The paper establishes sharp uniform and graph-specific bounds on the edge variation of the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator on finite connected graphs, and determines the optimal constant on star graphs for exponents above one.
summary.plain: The paper studies a way of averaging values on a network of points connected by edges, called a finite graph. It asks how much the averaged values can jump along edges compared with the original values. The authors find the best possible general constant for this, estimate the constant for each individual graph, and work out the exact answer for star-shaped graphs.
summary.why: The text is limited to the abstract, so its wider significance is unclear. It concerns discrete versions of a classical tool from analysis, the maximal operator, which is used in areas such as harmonic analysis and partial differential equations; any connection to those applications is not described in the text.

papers.abstract: We study edge variation for the centered Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator on finite connected graphs. We determine the optimal uniform coefficient controlling the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge variation of the original function and derive two-sided estimates for the variational constant of an individual graph. These estimates involve point-mass tests, the diameter, and the number of edges. On star graphs, we determine the sharp constant for exponents greater than one and characterize all nonconstant real-valued extremizers for every exponent.

papers.title: Variational Estimates for the Fractional Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24189v1

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges; "finite connected" means finitely many nodes, all reachable from one another.
- Maximal operator: replaces the value at a node with the largest (here, fractionally weighted) average over nearby nodes.
- Fractional exponent α with 0<α<1: weights decay with distance in a non-integer power, interpolating between local and global averaging.
- p-variation: a measure of how much a function changes along edges, using the p-th power of differences (p=∞ means the largest single jump).
- Sharp constant: the smallest coefficient that makes an inequality hold for all functions, shown with extremal examples.
- Complete graph: every pair of vertices is joined; star graph: one central vertex connected to all others.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves sharp edge-variation estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on finite connected graphs, including exact constants on complete and star graphs.
summary.plain: The paper studies a way of averaging values over nearby points on a network of nodes and connecting lines, where a fractional exponent controls how quickly distant points lose influence. It asks how much this averaging can make a function's changes along the edges grow, measured in a "variation" sense. The authors find exact best-possible constants for the uniform oscillation estimate, and for complete graphs and star graphs they compute sharp constants and show when certain bounds hold.
summary.why: The text gives exact constants for specific graph families and shows when a sharp bound holds, which gives concrete benchmarks for this kind of inequality. Its connection to wider analysis or applications is not spelled out in the text, so any broader significance is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We study edge variation estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on finite connected graphs. For $0<α<1$, we determine the optimal coefficient in the uniform estimate of the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge $p$-variation of the original function. We also obtain two-sided variation bounds involving the number of vertices and the diameter. On complete graphs, we prove that the sharp $(p,q)$ constant is $(1-n^{α-1})(n-1)^{1/q-1/p}$ for all $0<p\leq q\leq\infty$. On star graphs with $n\geq4$, we determine the sharp infinite-exponent constant and show that the sharp constant for $p=2$ equals $1-n^{α-1}$ if and only if $n^{α-1}\geq1/2$. Combining this with the known estimate for $p=1$, we also obtain sharp mixed estimates. Extremizers and counterexamples are given.

papers.title: Power loss for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi estimate on smooth hypersurfaces
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22465v1

summary.background:
- Fourier restriction: asking how well a function's Fourier transform (its decomposition into frequencies) can be restricted to a curved surface and still控制 its size.
- Hypersurface: a curved surface of one lower dimension inside a higher-dimensional space, such as a sphere or paraboloid.
- Second fundamental form: a measure of how strongly a surface bends at a point; nonzero means it is genuinely curved there.
- C^{2,β} smoothness: the surface has continuous second derivatives that are additionally Hölder continuous with exponent β, a precise notion of "slightly better than twice-differentiable".
- Local Mizohata–Takeuchi constant: the best constant in a localized weighted inequality bounding a surface integral of a Fourier transform by a volume-type integral; a conjecture predicted it stays bounded.
- Power-type lower bound: the constant must grow at least like a fixed power of some parameter, so it cannot stay bounded.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves power-type lower bounds for local Mizohata–Takeuchi constants on C^{2,β} hypersurfaces (0<β≤1) with nonvanishing second fundamental form at some point, thereby disproving the local Mizohata–Takeuchi conjectures for the paraboloid and the sphere.
summary.plain: This is a result in harmonic analysis, the mathematics of splitting functions into waves and studying how their energy is spread over curved surfaces. The authors study a weighted inequality tied to the Mizohata–Takeuchi problem for smooth curved surfaces such as the paraboloid and the sphere. They show that for a broad class of smooth surfaces the constants in this inequality must grow at least like a power, which rules out a conjectured bound for those two classic surfaces.
summary.why: The result shows that a general weighted approach to Fourier restriction problems for these classical surfaces cannot work in the form conjectured, so it narrows the set of available proof strategies. Its connection to broader Fourier restriction theory is stated in the text, but the wider implications beyond that are not spelled out here.

papers.abstract: We prove power-type lower bounds for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi constants for $C^{2,β}$ hypersurfaces with $0<β\leq1$ whose second fundamental form is nonzero at some point. This result, in particular, disproves the so-called local Mizohata--Takeuchi conjectures for the paraboloid and the sphere and, in turn, presents an obstruction to a general weighted approach to the theory of Fourier restriction of those classical surfaces.

papers.title: A counterexample to the one-supremum conjecture and sharp logarithmic weighted bounds for Calderón--Zygmund operators
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22097v1

summary.background:
- Calderón–Zygmund operators: a broad class of singular integral operators, including the Hilbert transform and Riesz transforms, central to harmonic analysis.
- Weights: nonnegative functions used to reweight measurements; a weighted norm measures how an operator behaves under this reweighting.
- A_p and A_infinity characteristics: numerical measures of how well-behaved a weight is; they are computed by averaging over cubes (small boxes), with A_p for the weight and A_infinity for its dual.
- Logarithmic loss: a bound that is off by a factor like (1+log A), which grows slowly but matters for sharp results.
- Conjecture: a proposed general inequality that the paper shows is false in a precise strong form.
- Research-level context: the paper relies on the setting of Hytönen–Lacey and Lerner–Moen; the text alone does not give the full proofs.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a negative answer to the one-supremum conjecture of Hytönen and Lacey (in the strong form stated by Lerner and Moen), by constructing weights for which a fixed Hilbert transform loses a logarithmic factor, and proves a logarithmically corrected weighted bound for Calderón–Zygmund operators.
summary.plain: This paper is about weighted inequalities: how much a standard averaging-type operator (a Calderón–Zygmund singular integral, such as the Hilbert transform) can amplify functions when each function is reweighted by a weight. A conjectured bound, stated in terms of two quantities each measured on a single cube, is shown to be false: the authors build explicit weights where the proposed bound fails even for one fixed Hilbert transform. They also prove a weaker bound with a logarithmic correction and argue that the correction exponent is the best possible.
summary.why: It settles a open question posed by experts in the area by showing the natural conjecture cannot hold, and it clarifies what information from a single cube can and cannot capture. Its connection to wider applications is not stated in the text, so I cannot say more than that it concerns sharp constants in weighted harmonic analysis.

papers.abstract: We give a negative answer to the one-supremum conjecture of Hytönen and Lacey~\cite[Remark~1.3]{HL}, in the strong-type form stated by Lerner and Moen~\cite[Conjecture~1.3, formula~(9)]{LM}. The conjecture asks whether the mixed $A_p$--$A_\infty$ characteristics $K_p(w)$ and $K_{p'}(σ)$, with both factors evaluated on the same cube, control Calderón--Zygmund operators without a logarithmic loss. For every $1<p<\infty$, we construct explicit weights for which $K_p(w)+K_{p'}(σ)\eqsim_p m$, but one fixed Hilbert transform has weighted norm at least $m(1+\log m)^{γ_p}$, where $γ_p=\max\{1/p,1/p'\}$. Thus the proposed bound fails even for a fixed singular integral. The counterexample also extends to a fixed Riesz transform in each dimension $n\ge2$. We further establish a logarithmically corrected bound for Calderón--Zygmund operators, with powers $1/p'$ and $1/p$ on the respective one-supremum terms. Together, the lower and upper bounds identify $γ_p$ as the optimal common logarithmic exponent and give the sharp worst-case growth $(1+\log A)^{γ_p}$ under the constraint $[w]_{A_p}\le A$. The results show why information from any one cube cannot fully capture the accumulation of a singular integral across many scales.

papers.title: The random KKM mapping principle and its applications
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18408v1

summary.background:
- Fixed point theorem: a result guaranteeing that a map from a set to itself has at least one point it leaves unchanged; Brouwer's theorem is the classic example.
- KKM principle: a combinatorial covering lemma (Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz) that underpins many fixed-point and minimax results.
- Minimax problem: finding a value that is simultaneously the best worst-case outcome for one player and the worst best-case for another.
- Variational inequality: a condition describing an equilibrium or optimum in optimization and economics.
- Compactness: a property of sets that roughly means they are closed and bounded in a finite-type sense; "noncompact" problems lack it, which is why standard theorems fail.
- L^0-modules: spaces of random variables, used to model randomness within functional analysis.
- Stable compactness: a technical notion from the paper's framework, not explained in the text.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a random version of the KKM mapping principle in Hausdorff topological L^0-modules, using the random Brouwer fixed point theorem and stable compactness, and derives fixed-point, minimax, variational inequality and conditional game results from it.
summary.plain: This paper is about extending a classic mathematical tool, the KKM principle (a covering-type result that guarantees certain points exist), to settings where the rules change randomly from one outcome to another. The authors build this version and use it to derive several existence results for fixed points, minimax problems, variational inequalities and conditional games. The text presents these as ways to handle problems that lack the usual compactness assumptions.
summary.why: Many economic, optimization and game-theory models involve randomness and infinite-dimensional spaces, where standard existence theorems often do not apply. The paper claims to cover a large class of such noncompact problems, though the abstract alone does not show how broad or practical that coverage is.

papers.abstract: Based on the recently developed random Brouwer fixed point theorem and the theory of stable compactness, we establish a random Knaster--Kuratowski--Mazurkiewicz (KKM) mapping principle in Hausdorff topological $L^0$-modules. As consequences of this principle, we obtain several results on fixed points, minimax problems, variational inequalities, and conditional games. These results solve a large class of noncompact problems in random functional analysis and its applications.

papers.title: Fourier Algebras of HLS Groupoids: Lifts, Amenability, and Spectrum
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21572v1

summary.background:
- Groupoid: a generalization of a group where composition is only defined for some pairs of elements.
- Locally compact / étale groupoid: groupoids with a topology that is locally well-behaved; étale means the structure is locally like a discrete space.
- Fourier algebra: an algebra of functions on a group or groupoid, generalizing the classical Fourier transform setting.
- Isotropy subgroup: the subgroup of elements that start and end at the same point.
- Eymard's theorem: a classical result identifying the spectrum of the Fourier algebra of a locally compact group with the group itself.
- Leptin's theorem: a classical result characterizing when the Fourier algebra has a bounded approximate identity (a near-unit with controlled size).
- Gelfand spectrum: the set of nonzero multiplicative functionals on a commutative algebra, which can be used to recover the underlying space.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies Fourier algebras of HLS groupoids within Paterson's framework, constructing norm-preserving lifts of restriction maps to isotropy subgroups, proving a Leptin-type bounded approximate identity criterion, and extending Eymard's theorem on the Gelfand spectrum to all étale groupoids.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a algebra of functions attached to a "groupoid," a mathematical structure that generalizes groups by allowing some pairs of elements to be unable to combine. For a special class of these structures (HLS groupoids), the authors describe the algebra concretely, show how its norms relate to simpler pieces called isotropy subgroups, and show its underlying space can be recovered from it. They also use more abstract arguments to extend some of these results to all étale groupoids, answering a question posed by Paterson.
summary.why: Fourier algebras link abstract group-like structures to analysis, and this work extends classical results such as Eymard's and Leptin's theorems to broader settings. The text does not say what applications beyond pure harmonic analysis it may have, so its wider reach is uncertain from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We investigate the Fourier algebra of a certain class of groupoids, called the HLS groupoids, within Paterson's continuous framework for locally compact groupoids. We develop the basic harmonic analysis of HLS groupoids by obtaining concrete descriptions of their topology, representations, and Fourier algebra. We then study the restriction maps from the Fourier algebra $A(\mathcal{G})$ of an HLS groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ to the Fourier algebras of its isotropy subgroups, and construct explicit norm-preserving lifts for these restriction maps. As applications, we describe the norm of every element of $A(\mathcal{G})$ in terms of the norms of its restrictions to the isotropy subgroups. We prove an analogue of Leptin's theorem characterizing when $A(\mathcal{G})$ has a bounded approximate identity. We also show that the Gelfand spectrum of $A(\mathcal{G})$ is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{G}$. Finally, using abstract arguments that, unlike our methods for HLS groupoids, do not yield explicit constructions, we show that norm-preserving lifts exist and that the Gelfand spectrum of the Fourier algebra is homeomorphic to the groupoid for every étale groupoid. This generalizes Eymard's theorem and answers a question of Paterson for étale groupoids.
